title: Assign Cookies
approach_name: Sort and match smallest sufficient cookie
notes:
Task: Maximize the number of children whose greed factor is met by a cookie.
Idea: Sort greed factors and cookie sizes, then assign the smallest sufficient cookie to each child in ascending greed order.
Invariant: Every accepted cookie satisfies the current least-greedy unmatched child, leaving larger cookies for later children.
Edge cases: If cookies run out, no further child can be satisfied; inputs may be empty.
time_complexity: O(n log n + m log m)
complexity_reason: Sorting both arrays dominates the two-pointer scan.

title: Assign Cookies
approach_name: Sort and match smallest sufficient cookie
notes:
Task: Satisfy as many children as possible using cookies that meet their greed factors.
Idea: Sort both arrays and use two pointers to match each child with the smallest cookie that is large enough.
Invariant: i counts children already satisfied, and j scans each cookie at most once.
Edge cases: Children left after the cookie array ends remain unsatisfied; empty arrays return zero.
time_complexity: O(n log n + m log m)
complexity_reason: Sorting is the dominant cost; matching uses a linear two-pointer scan.

title: 132 Pattern
notes:
Task: Detect indices i<j<k with nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j].
Idea: Scan from right to left, using a decreasing stack and a saved '2' candidate that is smaller than a prior stack value.
Invariant: third stores the largest feasible middle-low candidate found while scanning suffixes.
Edge cases: The stack contains possible '3' values; duplicate values do not satisfy the strict inequalities.
complexity_reason: Each value is pushed and popped at most once.

title: 132 Pattern
notes:
Task: Determine whether a 132 pattern exists with strict index and value inequalities.
Idea: Scan backward while a stack maintains possible high values and third tracks a feasible smaller middle value.
Invariant: If the current value is below third, it can serve as the pattern's first value.
Edge cases: Strict comparisons exclude equal values; an empty or short array returns false.
complexity_reason: Each element is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Circular Array Loop
notes:
Task: Determine whether the circular array has a cycle longer than one with a consistent direction.
Idea: Use slow/fast pointers and reject steps that change sign or return to the same index.
Invariant: Every valid pointer move follows the starting direction and remains in a cycle candidate.
Edge cases: One-element loops are invalid; failed paths are marked zero to avoid repeated work.
code:
class Solution:
    def circularArrayLoop(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        n=len(nums)
        def nxt(i,direction):
            if nums[i]*direction<0:return -1
            j=(i+nums[i])%n
            return -1 if j==i else j
        for start in range(n):
            if nums[start]==0:continue
            direction=1 if nums[start]>0 else -1;slow=fast=start
            while True:
                slow=nxt(slow,direction)
                if slow==-1:break
                fast=nxt(fast,direction)
                if fast==-1:break
                fast=nxt(fast,direction)
                if fast==-1:break
                if slow==fast:return True
            cur=start
            while nums[cur]*direction>0:
                j=(cur+nums[cur])%n;nums[cur]=0;cur=j
        return False
complexity_reason: Each failed path is zero-marked and pointer traversal is linear overall.

title: Circular Array Loop
notes:
Task: Find a circular cycle longer than one whose moves all have the same sign.
Idea: Run Floyd's slow/fast pointers while rejecting direction changes and single-index loops.
Invariant: Every accepted pointer transition follows the chosen direction and advances to another index.
Edge cases: Failed paths are zeroed to avoid repeat scans; the input is modified in place.
complexity_reason: Each unsuccessful path is marked and each index is explored only a bounded number of times.

title: Repeated Substring Pattern
notes:
Task: Determine whether s is a repetition of a proper substring.
Idea: Search for s inside the doubled string after removing its first and last characters.
Invariant: A nontrivial repeated pattern appears shifted somewhere within the overlap of s+s.
Edge cases: A single-character string returns false; the original string is assumed nonempty.
complexity_reason: The doubled string and substring search are linear in string length in typical implementations.

title: Repeated Substring Pattern
notes:
Task: Check whether the entire string consists of repeated copies of a shorter substring.
Idea: Search the original string in the doubled string with the first and last characters removed.
Invariant: If a repeated pattern exists, a nontrivial cyclic shift of the doubled string contains s.
Edge cases: A one-character string cannot match inside the shortened doubled string.
complexity_reason: The doubled string is linear in input length and substring search is typically linear.

title: Hamming Distance
notes:
Task: Count the bit positions where x and y differ.
Idea: XOR x and y, then count the set bits in the result.
Invariant: A bit in x^y is one exactly when the corresponding input bits differ.
Edge cases: Equal values produce zero; Python's bit_count counts set bits in the nonnegative XOR result.
complexity_reason: The XOR and population count use constant machine-word storage and work.

title: Hamming Distance
notes:
Task: Return the number of differing bit positions in two integers.
Idea: XOR the values and count the set bits.
Invariant: Every set bit in the XOR corresponds to one mismatch between x and y.
Edge cases: Identical integers return zero; Integer.bitCount handles the fixed-width representation.
complexity_reason: The implementation uses a fixed-width XOR and bit count.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements II
notes:
Task: Minimize the sum of absolute changes needed to make all values equal.
Idea: Sort the values and choose the middle value as a median, which minimizes total absolute distance.
Invariant: Every value contributes its absolute distance from the chosen median.
Edge cases: For even-length arrays, either middle value is a valid median; the implementation chooses the upper middle.
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates the linear sum of absolute differences.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements II
notes:
Task: Find the minimum total absolute increments/decrements to make all elements equal.
Idea: Sort and choose the middle element as a median; sum distances to it.
Invariant: The median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations in one dimension.
Edge cases: Either middle element works for an even number of values; long accumulation avoids intermediate overflow.
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates; the final pass sums distances.

title: Island Perimeter
notes:
Task: Compute the perimeter of a single island in a grid.
Idea: Add four edges for every land cell and subtract two for each shared land edge counted twice.
Invariant: The running perimeter equals all land-cell edges minus internal land-land shared edges.
Edge cases: Water cells contribute nothing; the grid may contain land cells touching the boundary.
complexity_reason: Each grid cell is inspected once and each shared edge is subtracted once.

title: Island Perimeter
notes:
Task: Return the perimeter of the island represented by land cells.
Idea: Count four edges per land cell, subtracting two when a land neighbor above or to the left shares an edge.
Invariant: Every shared edge is accounted for exactly once.
Edge cases: Water contributes no edges; the grid is scanned without modifying it.
complexity_reason: One scan visits every cell and uses constant auxiliary storage.

title: Can I Win
notes:
Task: Determine whether the first player can force the running total to reach desiredTotal first.
Idea: Memoize each set of chosen numbers as a bitmask and try every unused number as the next move.
Invariant: A state is winning if there exists a legal choice that immediately reaches the target or leaves the opponent a losing state.
Edge cases: If the sum of all available numbers is below desiredTotal, the first player cannot win; nonpositive desiredTotal is immediately won.
complexity_reason: Memoization considers subsets of m available numbers and scans possible moves per state.

title: Can I Win
notes:
Task: Check whether the first player has a forced win in the number-picking game.
Idea: Represent chosen values as a bitmask and memoize whether each state is winning.
Invariant: A state is winning if some unused choice reaches the target or moves to a losing opponent state.
Edge cases: If the sum of all choices is below desiredTotal, return false; nonpositive desiredTotal is already reached.
complexity_reason: There are at most 2^m masks and each state checks up to m choices.

title: Unique Substrings in Wraparound String
approach_name: Longest valid suffix per ending letter
notes:
Task: Count distinct substrings of p that occur in the infinite wraparound alphabet string.
Idea: Track the longest consecutive valid wraparound run ending at each letter.
Invariant: max_len[c] equals the longest valid substring ending with character c; it accounts for all distinct such suffixes.
Edge cases: The alphabet wraps from z to a; nonconsecutive characters reset the current run length.
complexity_reason: One scan updates a fixed 26-element array.

title: Unique Substrings in Wraparound String
approach_name: Longest valid suffix per ending letter
notes:
Task: Count distinct substrings that occur in the cyclic alphabet string.
Idea: For each ending character, store the maximum length of a contiguous wraparound substring ending there.
Invariant: If the longest valid suffix ending at a letter has length L, it contributes exactly L distinct substrings ending with that letter.
Edge cases: The transition from z to a is consecutive under modulo 26; other breaks reset run length to one.
complexity_reason: A single pass updates 26 fixed counters and one final sum completes the result.

title: Validate IP Address
notes:
Task: Classify a string as IPv4, IPv6, or Neither under strict component rules.
Idea: Validate four decimal IPv4 segments or eight hexadecimal IPv6 groups, checking length, characters, and leading-zero rules.
Invariant: A valid address has the exact component count and every component satisfies its protocol-specific syntax.
Edge cases: IPv4 segments cannot have leading zeros unless the segment is "0"; IPv6 groups contain one to four hexadecimal digits.
complexity_reason: The address is split and each character is checked a constant number of times.

title: Validate IP Address
notes:
Task: Validate an IPv4 or IPv6 address string, otherwise return Neither.
Idea: Split on the appropriate separator and validate every segment's length and character set.
Invariant: The address is accepted only if the exact number of components and all component constraints are satisfied.
Edge cases: IPv4 rejects leading zeros and values above 255; IPv6 allows one to four hexadecimal digits per group.
complexity_reason: The input is split and every character is validated once.
